title: The Marketing Fund Trap: The Levy Franchisors Collect but Don't Actually Own
excerpt: Royalty income and marketing fund contributions land in the same franchise transfer, but only one of them belongs to the franchisor. Here is why the difference matters most right before the Christmas campaign season.
content:
Every franchise invoice carries two different kinds of money, even though it lands as a single line. There is the royalty, the franchisor's actual income, calculated as a percentage of each site's revenue. And there is the marketing fund contribution, collected on the same invoice but earmarked for a specific, shared purpose: the national campaigns, the brand assets and the advertising spend that work better funded collectively than left to fifteen or fifty individual sites to organise on their own.

Both amounts land in the franchisor's bank account in the same transfer, on the same day, from the same franchisee. For whoever is running cash flow day to day, the pull to treat that combined deposit as one number is entirely understandable. It is also where the trouble usually starts.

The pattern across franchise systems is rarely deliberate. Nobody sets out to spend marketing fund money on general operating costs. It happens gradually, a quiet month covered by what looks like spare cash sitting in the account, repeated often enough that the fund balance and the actual bank balance drift apart without anyone noticing exactly when.

Two Pools of Cash, One Bank Account

Royalty income belongs to the franchisor outright, the same as any other revenue line, and can be spent, reinvested or distributed however the business sees fit. Marketing fund contributions are different in kind, not just in size. They are collected from franchisees for a defined purpose, and most franchise agreements are specific that the money can only be spent on marketing activity that benefits the network, not on the franchisor's own overheads, wages or working capital. Treating the two as a single pool of cash, even temporarily, blurs a line that franchisees, auditors and eventually the franchisor's own decision making all depend on staying clear. A structured approach to cash flow usually starts by separating these two pools before anything else, because every forecast built on top of a blended number inherits the same confusion.

Why the Gap Surfaces Right Before the Expensive Quarter

October is when most franchise marketing calendars tip into their heaviest spend of the year. Campaigns for the Christmas trading period need to be booked, paid and running well before December, and the marketing fund is the account those commitments draw from. If contributions collected through the quieter months have already been absorbed into general cash flow, the shortfall does not show up as an abstract accounting variance. It shows up as a franchisor short of the cash needed to pay for campaigns the network is expecting, at the exact moment franchisees are watching the most closely.

This is also the point in the year where franchisees start comparing what they paid into the fund against what they can see being spent on their behalf. A fund that has quietly run thin over the year is far harder to explain in November than it would have been to prevent in July.

What Franchisees Are Entitled to See

Under the Franchising Code of Conduct, a franchisor operating a marketing fund is required to prepare an annual financial statement showing how the money was spent and make it available to franchisees. That obligation exists because the fund is not discretionary income, it is money held for a defined group's benefit, and the reporting requirement is the mechanism that keeps that promise honest. Treating the annual statement as a compliance task to produce once a year, rather than a number that should be reconcilable at any point, is usually what leaves a franchisor scrambling to explain a shortfall they did not see coming.

Running the Marketing Fund Like Its Own Business

The franchise systems that avoid this keep the marketing fund on its own ledger, reconciled against contributions received and spend committed, reviewed with the same regularity as the rest of the business rather than once a year when the statement falls due. A quarterly financial health check that includes the marketing fund as a standing line item catches the drift while it is still a small number, well before it becomes the reason a Christmas campaign has to be scaled back or a franchisee asks a question the franchisor would rather not answer in writing.

None of this reflects badly on anyone running a franchise system. Royalty and marketing fund money arriving together in the same transfer is simply how the mechanics work, and untangling the two again is a structural job, not a judgement on how the business has been run. For a multi-site franchisor who has not looked at the marketing fund separately from general cash flow in some time, a fractional CFO brings that separation back into view before the next campaign season makes it urgent, and a discovery call is a reasonable place to start.

faqs.q: Can a franchisor spend marketing fund money on its own business costs?
faqs.a: Generally, no. Most franchise agreements specify that marketing fund contributions can only be spent on marketing activity that benefits the network, not on the franchisor's overheads or general working capital. Keeping the fund on a separate ledger is the simplest way to make sure that line never gets blurred.

faqs.q: What does the Franchising Code of Conduct require for marketing fund reporting?
faqs.a: A franchisor that operates a marketing fund must prepare an annual financial statement detailing how the money was spent and provide it to franchisees. The requirement exists because the fund is held for the network's benefit, not as discretionary franchisor income.

faqs.q: Why do franchise marketing funds often run short before Christmas?
faqs.a: Franchise marketing calendars typically peak in the lead-up to Christmas trading, when campaigns need to be booked and paid for well ahead of December. If contributions collected earlier in the year have already been drawn down for general cash flow, the fund can fall short exactly when the heaviest spending commitments land.

faqs.q: Should a franchisor keep royalty income and marketing fund contributions in separate accounts?
faqs.a: It is the cleanest way to avoid the two numbers blending into one. A structured cash flow approach treats the marketing fund as a distinct pool from day one, which makes the annual reporting obligation straightforward rather than a reconstruction exercise.

faqs.q: How often should a franchisor review its marketing fund balance?
faqs.a: Quarterly at minimum, alongside the rest of the network's financial reporting. A quarterly financial health check that treats the marketing fund as a standing line item picks up drift while the amount involved is still small and easy to correct.

faqs.q: What happens if a franchisor cannot account for marketing fund spending?
faqs.a: It damages trust with franchisees well before it becomes a compliance problem. Franchisees who contribute to a fund expect to see what it has paid for, and a franchisor who cannot reconcile the account is in a far weaker position in renewal and recruitment conversations than one who can.
